title: The One Partners In Health Clinic Not Built on Public Land
dek: In the mid-1980s Paul Farmer and Ophelia Dahl built a clinic in a Haitian squatter village, and learned later what a private clinic could not do.

story.event: Deciding to build a clinic for the poor in Cange, Haiti, and founding Partners In Health to support it
story.summary: After arriving in Haiti in 1983 and finding care for the poor mediocre, Paul Farmer chose to build a clinic in Cange, a squatter settlement of families displaced by the Péligre dam, working with the priest Fritz Lafontant and the English volunteer Ophelia Dahl and training local community health workers from 1984. With seed money from the Boston builder Tom White they founded Partners In Health in 1987. Dahl later said that first clinic was the only one of the organisation's facilities built off public land, and that it taught them to work with governments rather than build a parallel system.
paragraphs: In the spring of 1983, a year after leaving Duke University, Paul Farmer was in Haiti's Central Plateau. He was 23. With an Episcopal priest, Fritz Lafontant, he reached Cange, a squatter settlement of families whose valley farmland had been flooded by the Péligre hydroelectric dam. As Farmer later described it, there was no clinic, no clean water and no electricity, and the school met under a mango tree. That year Ophelia Dahl, a young Englishwoman, was volunteering at a small eye clinic in the same region; there she met Farmer.

Farmer had spent months visiting clinics, mobile clinics and hospitals, some well funded and run by people he respected. Care, he said, was "very mediocre for poor people at best." He had also watched short-term missions come and go. He resolved to stay and build in Cange: a clinic that would treat everyone, whatever they could pay, and would train local people to do much of the work. The first community health workers were recruited in 1984. That year he enrolled at Harvard Medical School, then took his books back to Haiti, returning for exams.

Money came in odd ways. A Boston anti-hunger charity paid for a bakery in Cange, which Farmer later called "probably not a good idea." Its anonymous donor was Tom White, a Boston builder, who visited and chose to back the work. Tracy Kidder later reported that Cange's first microscope had been appropriated from Harvard Medical School. A small clinic opened in the mid-1980s. In 1987, with Dahl, his Duke friend Todd McCormack and $1 million in seed money from White, Farmer set up Partners In Health in Boston, with Dahl as executive director. The name, Farmer said, came from wanting long-term partnerships, not visitors giving orders.

By 2000, Kidder found, the complex in Cange charged only nominal fees, and women, children and the seriously ill paid nothing. The first clinic also taught a limit. In 2012 Dahl said that of more than 60 facilities the organisation had since built or rebuilt, it was the only one not on public land. Seeing crowds converge on it, they realised: "we'll be building a parallel health system here if we don't start working with the government."

quote.text: Let thy house be open wide; let the poor be members of thy household
quote.thinker: Jose, son of Jochanan, of Jerusalem (in Pirkei Avot)
quote.source_title: Pirke Avot: The Sayings of the Jewish Fathers, tr. Joseph I. Gorfinkle, Project Gutenberg eBook #8547
quote.connection: Jose ben Jochanan asks for a private household opened wide to the poor, and Cange's first clinic was close to that. Dahl's later lesson was that one open house, however generous, can become a parallel system that lets the public one off the hook. The virtue and its limit both stand.

reflection: Farmer's first verdict on Haiti's clinics was harsh, and he later said that kind of diagnosis is the easy part. What he did next was slower: he stayed, trained neighbours as health workers, and kept working with the same people for decades. Even the bakery he regretted was part of staying.

Dahl's lesson is the quieter one. Doing good alongside a weak public system can, without anyone intending it, compete with it. Whatever you are building also sits inside larger structures: a hospital, a ministry, a family. It is fair to ask, on an unhurried day, whether your work strengthens those structures or routes around them.
invitation: Name one part of your work that runs alongside a bigger system rather than through it. Write down one person inside that system you could talk to this month, and leave the conversation itself for another day.

research_notes: The first clinic's date and size differ: the Academy of Achievement biography says Clinique Bon Saveur (usually spelled Bon Sauveur), a two-room clinic, opened in 1985; WBUR (2012) says Partners In Health got its start in 1987 when Farmer and Dahl helped set up a one-room clinic in Cange; Wikipedia gives 1983 for Zanmi Lasante's creation and 1985 for the building. The story says 'a small clinic opened in the mid-1980s' and dates only the founding of Partners In Health (1987, agreed by the Academy, WBUR and AP). Reach figures are not used because they conflict and describe different years: Kidder (2000) says about a million peasant farmers relied on the complex and about 100,000 lived in its catchment area; the Academy biography says it serves more than 150,000 people; Wikipedia says a catchment of 1.2 million. Fees: the 'nominal fees, free for women, children and the seriously ill' detail is Kidder's description of Zanmi Lasante in 2000 and is dated as such. Dahl's role: the Academy says she co-founded Zanmi Lasante with Farmer and Lafontant and became Partners In Health's executive director; Bending the Arc says she met Farmer while volunteering at the Eye Care Haiti clinic in 1983. Her age (18) appears only in a Wellesley page that no longer loads, so it is not given. Farmer's quotations come from his Academy of Achievement interview, recorded in Cape Town (he refers to the four hurricanes of 'last year', so 2009). The microscope anecdote is Kidder's wording ('appropriated'), attributed to him. The New York Times obituary and Partners In Health's own pages return 403 to the verifier and were not cited. The quoted saying is the first half of Avot 1:5; the omitted remainder (on gossip) is not spliced. Tracy Kidder's Mountains Beyond Mountains (2003) is the fuller account but was not available in a lawful, loadable copy.
